questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Volatility invalidates a simplified total-vapour inference but not a sealed retained-solute osmotic measurement
questions.syllabus_anchor: Solutions: vapour pressure; osmotic pressure; molar-mass determination
questions.question: A sealed dilute solution contains 10.0 g of a molecular solute per litre and has osmotic pressure π=0.100 RT in consistent litre–mole units. Its membrane passes only solvent. The solute is volatile and contributes to the total equilibrium vapour pressure. Which inference is justified?
options: A) Osmotic molar mass is 100 g mol−1; the simple nonvolatile-solute vapour-pressure-lowering formula cannot be used on total pressure
B) Osmotic molar mass is negative because total vapour pressure can exceed the pure solvent pressure
C) Volatility alone makes the retained-solute osmotic measurement impossible
D) Both measurements must give 10.0 g mol−1 without accounting for solute vapour
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The osmotic result is usable under the stated membrane condition; total vapour pressure requires both components.
Given: The vessel is sealed and the membrane excludes the solute, preventing loss or leakage from invalidating the stated concentration.
Formula/Principle: \(\pi=cRT\) for the dilute molecular solution, while volatile-component total pressure is the sum of both partial pressures.
Step 1: \[c=\pi/(RT)=0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}.\]
Step 2: \[M=\frac{10.0\ \mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}}{0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}}=100\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}.\]
Why: The nonvolatile-solute lowering formula assumes the solute does not itself supply vapour pressure. That assumption is distinct from solute exclusion by an osmotic membrane.
Why not the others: (B) converts failure of an inappropriate vapour formula into an impossible mass. (C) ignores the explicit retention and sealed-system assumptions. (D) neither follows the osmotic division nor includes solute vapour.
Key point: Check the separate physical assumptions of two colligative measurements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Impure oxidant and combustion products jointly fix empirical ratio and excess oxygen
questions.syllabus_anchor: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry: empirical formula; combustion; limiting reagents
questions.question: Complete combustion of 0.800 g of a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen gives 0.0500 mol CO2 and 0.100 mol H2O. The oxidant feed contains 0.150 mol total gas, 80.0 percent O2 and 20.0 percent inert gas; all carbon and hydrogen reach the stated products. What are the empirical formula and residual O2 amount? Use C=12,H=1.
options: A) CH2; 0.0450 mol
B) CH4; 0.0500 mol
C) CH4; 0.0200 mol
D) C2H4; 0.120 mol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) CH4 and 0.0200 mol oxygen remaining.
Given: The oxidant's stated total includes inert gas.
Formula/Principle: Product atom balances determine empirical composition and actual oxygen consumption.
Step 1: Carbon is 0.0500 mol and hydrogen atoms are 2(0.100)=0.200 mol, giving C:H=1:4. Their masses sum to \(0.0500(12)+0.200(1)=0.800\) g, checking the sample.
Step 2: Product oxygen demand is \[n_{O_2}=n_{CO_2}+\tfrac12n_{H_2O}=0.0500+0.0500=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}.\]
Step 3: Available oxygen is \(0.150(0.800)=0.120\) mol, leaving \[0.120-0.100=0.0200\ \mathrm{mol}.\]
Why: Oxygen is in excess and the organic sample is completely consumed. Counting inert feed as oxygen would overstate the excess.
Why not the others: (A) forgets the two hydrogen atoms per water molecule. (B) treats the entire feed as oxygen. (D) does not reduce the empirical ratio and ignores oxygen consumption.
Key point: Separate feed composition from reaction stoichiometry.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.sub_topic: The argon–potassium mass inversion tests the actual variable in the modern periodic law
questions.syllabus_anchor: Classification of Elements: modern periodic law; atomic number
questions.question: Argon has atomic number 18 and relative atomic mass about 39.95; potassium has atomic number 19 and mass about 39.10. Which placement is consistent with the modern periodic law?
options: A) Potassium precedes argon because its relative atomic mass is lower
B) Argon precedes potassium because atomic number, not atomic mass, defines the modern ordering
C) They occupy one position because both masses are close to 40
D) Their order depends on how many neutrons a particular isotope contains
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Atomic numbers 18 then 19 fix argon before potassium.
Why: The modern periodic law relates periodic properties to atomic number. Relative atomic mass is an abundance-weighted isotopic property and need not increase in the same order for every adjacent pair. Argon–potassium illustrates why a mass-only ordering cannot replace the nuclear-charge ordering. Isotopes of the same element retain its atomic number and therefore do not receive separate periodic-table positions.
Why not the others: (A) reapplies an atomic-mass criterion instead of the modern law. (C) treats approximate mass equality as equality of element identity. (D) uses neutron count where nuclear charge is required.
Key point: Keep elemental ordering distinct from isotopic mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Vitamin solubility predicts absorption vulnerability without an absolute rule about all water-soluble stores
questions.syllabus_anchor: Biomolecules: vitamins; water- and fat-soluble groups
questions.question: A model compares prolonged impairment of fat absorption with a short period of low vitamin-C intake. Which statement best uses vitamin solubility without claiming that every water-soluble vitamin has identical storage behaviour?
options: A) All vitamins are stored equally, so solubility cannot affect deficiency risk
B) Vitamin C must require fat absorption because its name includes a letter
C) Fat malabsorption selectively prevents absorption of B vitamins but leaves A,D,E,K unaffected
D) Fat-soluble A,D,E,K are particularly vulnerable to impaired fat absorption; vitamin-C intake and limited reserves can produce a different time course
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Solubility influences absorption and storage, but does not impose one universal deficiency timetable.
Why: Vitamins A,D,E and K are fat soluble and can be affected when fat absorption is impaired. Vitamin C is water soluble and is not stored in the same way as typical fat-soluble reserves, so inadequate intake may produce a different time course. Water solubility must not be turned into an exceptionless statement that every B vitamin has no significant stores; vitamin B12 is an important storage exception. The question concerns the supported class distinction rather than diagnosing a specific patient from duration alone.
Why not the others: (A) removes meaningful absorption and storage differences. (B) classifies chemistry from a name. (C) reverses the solubility-related absorption vulnerability.
Key point: Use solubility as a biological constraint while retaining known exceptions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Both conjugate-ion hydrolyses determine the pH of a weak-acid weak-base salt
questions.syllabus_anchor: Equilibrium: ionic equilibrium; hydrolysis of salts
questions.question: A 0.100 M salt BH+A− is formed from weak base B with Kb=10−6 and weak acid HA with Ka=10−4. At 25 degrees C take Kw=10−14 and use the usual weak-acid/weak-base salt hydrolysis approximation. What pH and interpretation follow?
options: A) Approximately 6; BH+ acidity exceeds the basic influence of A−
B) Exactly 7; every 1:1 salt must be neutral
C) Approximately 8; the weaker parent base makes its conjugate acid weaker
D) Approximately 4; the salt behaves as 0.100 M strong acid
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The salt is acidic, with approximate pH 6.
Given: Parent-base Kb=10⁻⁶ and parent-acid Ka=10⁻⁴.
Formula/Principle: Both ions hydrolyse; \(pH=7+\tfrac12\log(K_b/K_a)\) under the specified approximation.
Step 1: Their separate constants are \[K_a(BH^+)=K_w/K_b=10^{-8},\quad K_b(A^-)=K_w/K_a=10^{-10}.\] The cation's acidic action is stronger.
Step 2: \[pH=7+\tfrac12\log(10^{-6}/10^{-4})=7-1=6.\]
Why: Equal stoichiometric charges do not mean equal acid and base strengths. Both parent equilibria, not only the 1:1 salt formula, determine hydrolysis.
Why not the others: (B) confuses electrical neutrality with neutral pH. (C) reverses the conjugate-strength relation and the logarithmic ratio. (D) treats weak hydrolysis as complete strong-acid dissociation.
Key point: Recover both conjugate-ion constants before interpreting a weak/weak salt.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Parallel tangency and a horizontal-width parabolic segment integral
questions.syllabus_anchor: Coordinate Geometry: parabola; tangents; Integral Calculus: areas
questions.question: For the parabola y²=4x, A=(1,2) and B=(9,6). What are the point at which the tangent is parallel to AB and the area of the parabolic segment bounded by AB and the parabola?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (4,4); 8/3.
Given: \(y^2=4x,\quad A(1,2),\quad B(9,6)\)
Formula/Principle: \(2y\,y'=4\Rightarrow y'=\dfrac2y;\quad\text{area}=\displaystyle\int_{y_A}^{y_B}\left(x_{\text{chord}}-x_{\text{parabola}}\right)dy\)
Step 1: \(m_{AB}=\dfrac{6-2}{9-1}=\dfrac12\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac2y=\dfrac12\Rightarrow y=4,\quad x=\dfrac{16}4=4\)
Step 3: \(AB:\ y-2=\tfrac12(x-1)\Rightarrow x=2y-3\)
Step 4: \(\text{area}=\displaystyle\int_2^6\left(2y-3-\frac{y^2}4\right)dy=\left[y^2-3y-\frac{y^3}{12}\right]_2^6\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{area}=(36-18-18)-\left(4-6-\tfrac23\right)=0+\tfrac83=\tfrac83\]
Check: \[\triangle\,(1,2),(9,6),(4,4):\ \tfrac12|1(6-4)+9(4-2)+4(2-6)|=2;\quad\tfrac43\times2=\tfrac83\ \ (\text{Archimedes})\]
Why: \(2y-3-\tfrac{y^2}4=-\tfrac14(y-2)(y-6)\ge0\ \text{on}\ [2,6]\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac43=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac83\); (C) \((2,2):\ 4\ne8\); (D) \(\tfrac{16}3=2\cdot\tfrac83\).
Key point: \(\text{parabolic segment}=\tfrac43\times\text{triangle with vertex at the parallel tangent}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Outer stationary preimages and an inner derivative zero contribute different extrema
questions.syllabus_anchor: Differentiation: chain rule; stationary points; sign analysis
questions.question: A differentiable f on (-1,∞) has f'(u)=(u-1)/(u+1). Let g(x)=f(x²) for all real x. Which classification of g's stationary points is correct?
options: A) Only x=0 is stationary, and it is a minimum
B) Only x=±1 are stationary, both maxima
C) There are two maxima and one minimum
D) There is a maximum at 0 and minima at -1 and 1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) There is a maximum at 0 and minima at -1 and 1.
Given: \(f'(u)=\dfrac{u-1}{u+1},\quad g(x)=f(x^2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(g'(x)=f'(x^2)\cdot2x\)
Step 1: \(g'(x)=\dfrac{2x(x^2-1)}{x^2+1}=\dfrac{2x(x-1)(x+1)}{x^2+1}\)
Step 2: \(g'(x)=0\Rightarrow x=-1,\ 0,\ 1\)
Step 3: \(x<-1:\ g'<0;\quad-1<x<0:\ g'>0;\quad0<x<1:\ g'<0;\quad x>1:\ g'>0\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\pm1:\ (-\to+)\ \text{minima};\qquad x=0:\ (+\to-)\ \text{maximum}\]
Check: \[g'(-2)=\tfrac{-12}5<0,\ g'\left(-\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac{(-1)(-3/4)}{5/4}=\tfrac35>0,\ g'\left(\tfrac12\right)=-\tfrac35<0,\ g'(2)=\tfrac{12}5>0\]
Why: \(\text{the factor}\ 2x\ \text{from the inner function gives the extra stationary point}\ x=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(g'(\pm1)=0\ \text{also, and}\ x=0\ \text{is a maximum}\); (B) \(g'(0)=0\ \text{also, and}\ \pm1\ \text{are minima}\); (C) \(\text{one maximum, two minima}\).
Key point: \((f\circ h)'=f'(h)\,h'\ \text{vanishes when either factor does}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Two integration-by-parts terms and endpoint accounting after translation
questions.syllabus_anchor: Integral Calculus: substitution; integration by parts
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x\ln(1+x)}{(1+x)^3}\,dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (5-6 ln 2)/16.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x\ln(1+x)}{(1+x)^3}\,dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(u=1+x;\quad\displaystyle\int\frac{\ln u}{u^2}du=-\frac{\ln u+1}u,\quad\int\frac{\ln u}{u^3}du=-\frac{\ln u}{2u^2}-\frac1{4u^2}\)
Step 1: \(I=\displaystyle\int_1^2\frac{(u-1)\ln u}{u^3}du=\int_1^2\frac{\ln u}{u^2}du-\int_1^2\frac{\ln u}{u^3}du=I_1-I_2\)
Step 2: \(I_1=\left[-\dfrac{\ln u+1}u\right]_1^2=-\dfrac{\ln2+1}2+1=\dfrac{1-\ln2}2\)
Step 3: \(I_2=\left[-\dfrac{\ln u}{2u^2}-\dfrac1{4u^2}\right]_1^2=-\dfrac{\ln2}8-\dfrac1{16}+\dfrac14=\dfrac3{16}-\dfrac{\ln2}8\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac12-\frac{\ln2}2-\frac3{16}+\frac{\ln2}8=\frac5{16}-\frac{3\ln2}8=\frac{5-6\ln2}{16}\approx0.053\]
Check: \[\frac d{du}\left(-\frac{\ln u+1}u\right)=-\frac1{u^2}+\frac{\ln u+1}{u^2}=\frac{\ln u}{u^2};\quad0<I<\max\frac{x\ln(1+x)}{(1+x)^3}<\frac{\ln2}{4}\approx0.17\]
Why: \(x=u-1\ \text{splits the integrand into two standard forms}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac{1-\ln2}2=I_1\ \text{only}\); (C) \(\tfrac{5-2\ln2}{16}\approx0.226\ne0.053\); (D) \(\tfrac{3-2\ln2}{16}=I_2\ \text{only}\).
Key point: \(\text{shift}\ u=1+x,\ \text{then integrate by parts}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting symmetric transitive relations uses inactive elements and vacuous cases rather than adding closure pairs
questions.syllabus_anchor: Relations and Functions: symmetric; transitive; reflexive; equivalence relations
questions.question: How many relations on A={1,2,3} are symmetric and transitive but are not reflexive on A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10.
Given: \(A=\{1,2,3\};\quad R\ \text{symmetric and transitive, not reflexive}\)
Formula/Principle: \((a,b)\in R\Rightarrow(b,a)\in R\Rightarrow(a,a),(b,b)\in R;\quad R=\text{equivalence relation on a subset}\ S\subsetneq A\)
Step 1: \(|S|=0:\ R=\varnothing\Rightarrow1\)
Step 2: \(|S|=1:\ \dbinom31\times B_1=3\times1=3\)
Step 3: \(|S|=2:\ \dbinom32\times B_2=3\times2=6\)
Step 4: \(|S|=3:\ B_3=5\ \text{(reflexive, excluded)}\)
Worked derivation: \[N=1+3+6=10\]
Check: \[\sum_{k=0}^3\binom3kB_k=1+3+6+5=15=B_4;\quad15-5=10\]
Why: \(\text{an element in no pair breaks reflexivity but not symmetry or transitivity}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3\ \text{counts}\ |S|=1\ \text{only}\); (B) \(6\ \text{counts}\ |S|=2\ \text{only}\); (D) \(15\ \text{includes the 5 equivalence relations on}\ A\).
Key point: \(\text{symmetric}+\text{transitive}=\text{equivalence relation on the set of elements used}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A dependent row constrains consistency before the solution family is counted
questions.syllabus_anchor: Matrices: elementary row reasoning; linear equations
questions.question: The equations x+2y+z=3, 2x+4y+2z=a and z=1 are considered over the real numbers. For which a is the system consistent, and how many solutions does it then have?
options: A) a=6; infinitely many
B) a=3; one
C) a=6; one
D) No a; the singular coefficient matrix is always inconsistent
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) a=6; infinitely many.
Given: \(x+2y+z=3,\quad2x+4y+2z=a,\quad z=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(R_2-2R_1:\ 0=a-6\)
Step 1: \(\text{consistent}\iff a=6\)
Step 2: \(z=1\Rightarrow x+2y=2\)
Step 3: \(y=t\Rightarrow x=2-2t\)
Worked derivation: \[(x,y,z)=(2-2t,\ t,\ 1),\quad t\in\mathbb R\ \Rightarrow\ \text{infinitely many solutions}\]
Check: \[t=0:\ (2,0,1):\ 2+0+1=3,\ 4+0+2=6;\qquad\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}[A|b]=2<3\]
Why: \(\det A=0\Rightarrow\text{no unique solution; either none or infinitely many}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(a=3:\ 0=-3\); (C) \(\operatorname{rank}=2<3\Rightarrow\text{one free parameter}\); (D) \(a=6\ \text{is consistent}\).
Key point: \(\text{dependent rows need the same dependence on the right-hand side}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A second-failure stopping condition reweights unequal-probability prefixes
questions.syllabus_anchor: Probability: conditional probability; independent events
questions.question: Independent Bernoulli trials are performed until the second failure. Success probabilities on trials 1,2,3 are 1/2,2/3,3/4; the fourth trial has a nonzero failure probability. Given that stopping occurs exactly on trial 4, what is the probability trial 1 was a success?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5/11.
Given: \(P(S_1)=\tfrac12,\ P(S_2)=\tfrac23,\ P(S_3)=\tfrac34;\quad\text{stop at the 2nd failure, on trial 4}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\{T=4\}=\{\text{exactly one }F\text{ in trials 1–3}\}\cap\{F_4\};\quad P(S_1\mid T=4)=\dfrac{P(S_1\cap T=4)}{P(T=4)}\)
Step 1: \(P(FSS)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac14\)
Step 2: \(P(SFS)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac18\)
Step 3: \(P(SSF)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac1{12}\)
Step 4: \(P(F_4)=p_4\ \text{multiplies numerator and denominator}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(S_1\mid T=4)=\frac{\left(\tfrac18+\tfrac1{12}\right)p_4}{\left(\tfrac14+\tfrac18+\tfrac1{12}\right)p_4}=\frac{5/24}{11/24}=\frac5{11}\]
Check: \[P(F_1\mid T=4)=\frac{6/24}{11/24}=\frac6{11};\quad\frac5{11}+\frac6{11}=1\]
Why: \(\text{the three allowed prefixes are not equally likely}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac23=\tfrac{2\ \text{patterns}}{3\ \text{patterns}}\ (\text{unweighted})\); (C) \(\tfrac12=P(S_1)\ (\text{unconditioned})\); (D) \(\tfrac3{11}=\tfrac{1/8}{11/24}\ (\text{omits}\ SSF)\).
Key point: \(\text{weight each pattern by its own probability before conditioning}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Alternating digit sums and leading-zero exclusion constrain a full digit permutation
questions.syllabus_anchor: Permutations and Combinations: restricted counting
questions.question: How many five-digit positive integers use each digit 0,1,2,3,4 exactly once and are divisible by 11?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 16.
Given: \(\text{digits}\ 0,1,2,3,4\ \text{once each};\quad d_1\ne0\)
Formula/Principle: \(11\mid N\iff(d_1+d_3+d_5)-(d_2+d_4)\equiv0\pmod{11}\)
Step 1: \(S=d_1+d_3+d_5,\quad d_2+d_4=10-S\Rightarrow2S-10\equiv0\pmod{11}\)
Step 2: \(3\le S\le9\Rightarrow-4\le2S-10\le8\Rightarrow2S-10=0\Rightarrow S=5\)
Step 3: \(\{d_1,d_3,d_5\}=\{0,1,4\}\ \text{or}\ \{0,2,3\}\)
Step 4: \(\text{each set}:\ 3!\times2!=12\ \text{arrangements};\quad d_1=0:\ 2!\times2!=4\)
Worked derivation: \[N=2\times(12-4)=16\]
Check: \[13024=11\times1184:\quad(1+0+4)-(3+2)=0\]
Why: \(\text{both admissible sets contain}\ 0,\ \text{so each loses its leading-zero arrangements}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(24=2\times12\ (\text{leading zeros kept})\); (B) \(12\ (\text{one set, uncorrected})\); (C) \(20=24-4\ (\text{only one set corrected})\).
Key point: \(\text{alternating digit sums must differ by a multiple of 11}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: One shared binomial coefficient fixes an integer exponent but not a later coefficient
questions.syllabus_anchor: Binomial Theorem: coefficients; positive integral exponents
questions.question: For an integer n≥4, the coefficients of x² in (1+x)^n and (1+√5 x)^(n-3) are equal. What is the coefficient of x³ in the first expansion minus that in the second?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 20-5√5.
Given: \([x^2](1+x)^n=[x^2](1+\sqrt5x)^{n-3},\quad n\ge4\)
Formula/Principle: \([x^r](1+ax)^m=\dbinom mra^r\)
Step 1: \(\dbinom n2=5\dbinom{n-3}2\Rightarrow n(n-1)=5(n-3)(n-4)\)
Step 2: \(n^2-n=5n^2-35n+60\Rightarrow2n^2-17n+30=0\Rightarrow(2n-5)(n-6)=0\)
Step 3: \(n\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow n=6\)
Step 4: \([x^3](1+x)^6=\dbinom63=20\)
Step 5: \([x^3](1+\sqrt5x)^3=\dbinom33(\sqrt5)^3=5\sqrt5\)
Worked derivation: \[20-5\sqrt5\approx8.82\]
Check: \[\binom62=15=5\binom32=5\times3\]
Why: \(n=\tfrac52\ \text{is not an integer}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(20+5\sqrt5\ (\text{sum})\); (C) \((\sqrt5)^3=5\sqrt5\ne\sqrt5\); (D) \(5\sqrt5-20\ (\text{order reversed})\).
Key point: \(\text{the factor}\ a^r\ \text{changes with the power compared}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Odd-integer arithmetic and square sums determine an integer term count
questions.syllabus_anchor: Sequences and Series: arithmetic sums; sums of squares
questions.question: The sum of squares of the first n positive odd integers is two less than eight times their sum. What is the positive integer n?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6.
Given: \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-1)^2=8\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-1)-2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-1)=n^2,\quad\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-1)^2=\frac{n(4n^2-1)}3\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{n(4n^2-1)}3=8n^2-2\)
Step 2: \(4n^3-n=24n^2-6\Rightarrow4n^3-24n^2-n+6=0\)
Step 3: \(4n^2(n-6)-(n-6)=0\Rightarrow(n-6)(4n^2-1)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[n=6\quad\left(n=\pm\tfrac12\ \text{rejected}\right)\]
Check: \[1+9+25+49+81+121=286;\quad8\times36-2=286\]
Why: \(n\ \text{counts terms}\Rightarrow n\in\mathbb Z^+\)
Why not the others: (A) \(n=4:\ 84\ne126\); (B) \(n=5:\ 165\ne198\); (D) \(n=8:\ 680\ne510\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-1)^2=\frac{n(2n-1)(2n+1)}3\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A unique removable extension is differentiable but cannot repair an oscillating neighbouring derivative
questions.syllabus_anchor: Limits and Continuity; Differentiation: derivative definition; product rule
questions.question: Let f(x)=x² sin(1/x) for x≠0 and f(0)=a. Which statement about extension at zero is complete?
options: A) For a=0, f'(0)=0 and f' is continuous at zero
B) For a=0, f'(0)=0 but f' is not continuous there; no a makes the extension continuously differentiable at zero
C) No a makes f differentiable at zero
D) Every a makes f continuous, but none makes it differentiable
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) For a=0, f'(0)=0 but f' is not continuous there; no a makes the extension continuously differentiable at zero.
Given: \(f(x)=x^2\sin\tfrac1x\ (x\ne0),\quad f(0)=a\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(0)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}h;\quad f'\ \text{continuous at}\ 0\iff\lim_{x\to0}f'(x)=f'(0)\)
Step 1: \(\left|x^2\sin\tfrac1x\right|\le x^2\to0\Rightarrow\text{continuity needs}\ a=0\)
Step 2: \(f'(0)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}h\sin\tfrac1h=0\quad\left(|h\sin\tfrac1h|\le|h|\right)\)
Step 3: \(x\ne0:\ f'(x)=2x\sin\tfrac1x-\cos\tfrac1x\)
Step 4: \(x_n=\dfrac1{2n\pi}:\ f'(x_n)=-1;\qquad x_n=\dfrac1{(2n+1)\pi}:\ f'(x_n)=+1\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(0)=0,\qquad\lim_{x\to0}f'(x)\ \text{does not exist}\ (-1\ne+1)\]
Check: \[a\ne0:\ \lim_{x\to0}f(x)=0\ne a\Rightarrow\text{not continuous}\Rightarrow\text{not differentiable}\]
Why: \(\text{the choice of}\ a\ \text{cannot change}\ f'(x)\ \text{for}\ x\ne0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\lim f'\ \text{does not exist}\); (C) \(a=0\Rightarrow f'(0)=0\); (D) \(\text{continuity needs}\ a=0,\ \text{and then}\ f'(0)\ \text{exists}\).
Key point: \(\text{differentiable at a point does not imply}\ f'\ \text{continuous there}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Separation loses a family of trigonometric equilibria unless checked first
questions.syllabus_anchor: Differential Equations: separation of variables; constant solutions
questions.question: Consider y'=sin y on the real line. Which are its constant solutions, and for the nonconstant solution with y(0)=π/2 and 0<y<π, what is y(ln√3)?
options: A) Only y=0; value π/3
B) All y=nπ with integer n; value π/3
C) Only y=π; value 2π/3
D) All y=nπ with integer n; value 2π/3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) All y=nπ with integer n; value 2π/3.
Given: \(y'=\sin y,\quad y(0)=\tfrac\pi2,\quad0<y<\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int\csc y\,dy=\ln\left|\tan\tfrac y2\right|+C\)
Step 1: \(y=c\ \text{constant}\Rightarrow\sin c=0\Rightarrow c=n\pi,\ n\in\mathbb Z\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dy}{\sin y}=dx\Rightarrow\ln\tan\tfrac y2=x+C\)
Step 3: \(y(0)=\tfrac\pi2:\ \ln\tan\tfrac\pi4=0=C\Rightarrow\tan\tfrac y2=e^x\)
Step 4: \(x=\ln\sqrt3:\ \tan\tfrac y2=\sqrt3\Rightarrow\tfrac y2=\tfrac\pi3\)
Worked derivation: \[y(\ln\sqrt3)=\tfrac{2\pi}3;\qquad\text{constant solutions}\ y=n\pi\]
Check: \[y=2\arctan e^x:\ y'=\frac{2e^x}{1+e^{2x}}=\frac{2\tan\frac y2}{1+\tan^2\frac y2}=\sin y\]
Why: \(0<\tfrac y2<\tfrac\pi2\ \text{fixes the branch of}\ \arctan\)
Why not the others: (A) \(y=\pi,\ 2\pi,\dots\ \text{are also constant solutions};\ \tfrac\pi3\ne\tfrac{2\pi}3\); (B) \(\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac y2,\ \text{not}\ y\); (C) \(y=0,\ 2\pi,\dots\ \text{are also constant solutions}\).
Key point: \(\text{list the zeros of the right-hand side before dividing by it}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: An oblique prescribed direction changes the point-plane connecting distance
questions.syllabus_anchor: Three-dimensional Geometry: line-plane intersection; distance
questions.question: From P=(1,2,3), a line parallel to (1,0,1) meets the plane x+y+z=0 at Q. What are Q and the distance PQ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (-2,2,0); 3√2.
Given: \(P(1,2,3),\quad\vec d=(1,0,1),\quad x+y+z=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q=P+t\vec d,\quad PQ=|t|\,|\vec d|\)
Step 1: \(Q=(1+t,\ 2,\ 3+t)\)
Step 2: \((1+t)+2+(3+t)=0\Rightarrow2t=-6\Rightarrow t=-3\)
Step 3: \(Q=(-2,2,0)\)
Worked derivation: \[PQ=3\sqrt{1^2+0^2+1^2}=3\sqrt2\]
Check: \[-2+2+0=0;\quad PQ^2=(1+2)^2+(2-2)^2+(3-0)^2=18\]
Why: \(\text{the distance is measured along}\ \vec d,\ \text{not along the normal}\)
Why not the others: (B) \((-1,0,1),\ 2\sqrt3:\ \text{foot of the perpendicular}\); (C) \(0+2+2=4\ne0\); (D) \(2\sqrt3=\tfrac{|1+2+3|}{\sqrt3}\ (\text{perpendicular distance})\).
Key point: \(\text{substitute the parametric point into the plane}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A free parallel component in a cross-product equation is fixed by minimum norm
questions.syllabus_anchor: Vector Algebra: vector product; perpendicular components
questions.question: Let a=(1,1,0) and require a×v=(0,0,2). What is the minimum possible squared magnitude |v|² over all real solutions?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: \(\mathbf a=(1,1,0),\quad\mathbf a\times\mathbf v=(0,0,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf a\times\mathbf v=(a_2v_3-a_3v_2,\ a_3v_1-a_1v_3,\ a_1v_2-a_2v_1)\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf v=(x,y,z):\ \mathbf a\times\mathbf v=(z,\ -z,\ y-x)\)
Step 2: \(z=0,\quad y-x=2\Rightarrow\mathbf v=(t,\ t+2,\ 0)\)
Step 3: \(|\mathbf v|^2=t^2+(t+2)^2=2t^2+4t+4=2(t+1)^2+2\)
Worked derivation: \[|\mathbf v|^2_{\min}=2\ \ \text{at}\ t=-1,\quad\mathbf v=(-1,1,0)\]
Check: \[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v=-1+1=0;\quad|\mathbf a\times\mathbf v|=|\mathbf a||\mathbf v|\Rightarrow2=\sqrt2\,|\mathbf v|\Rightarrow|\mathbf v|^2=2\]
Why: \(\text{a component of}\ \mathbf v\ \text{along}\ \mathbf a\ \text{adds length but no cross product}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1<2\ (\text{below the minimum})\); (B) \(4=|(0,2,0)|^2\ (t=0)\); (D) \(\mathbf v=0\Rightarrow\mathbf a\times\mathbf v=0\).
Key point: \(|\mathbf v|_{\min}=\dfrac{|\mathbf a\times\mathbf v|}{|\mathbf a|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A grouped population variance gives two real roots but only one valid integer frequency
questions.syllabus_anchor: Statistics: grouped data; mean; variance
questions.question: Grouped classes [0,2),[2,4),[4,6) have frequencies a,2,1. Use class midpoints and population variance. If a is a nonnegative integer and the variance is 56/25, what are a and the mean?
options: B) a=2; mean 13/5
C) a=2; mean 3
D) a=1; mean 3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) a=2; mean 13/5.
Given: \(x_i=1,3,5;\quad f_i=a,2,1;\quad\sigma^2=\tfrac{56}{25}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar x=\dfrac{\sum f_ix_i}{\sum f_i},\quad\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum f_ix_i^2}{\sum f_i}-\bar x^2\)
Step 1: \(\bar x=\dfrac{a+6+5}{a+3}=\dfrac{a+11}{a+3},\quad\dfrac{\sum f_ix_i^2}{\sum f_i}=\dfrac{a+18+25}{a+3}=\dfrac{a+43}{a+3}\)
Step 2: \(\sigma^2=\dfrac{(a+43)(a+3)-(a+11)^2}{(a+3)^2}=\dfrac{24a+8}{(a+3)^2}\)
Step 3: \(25(24a+8)=56(a+3)^2\Rightarrow56a^2-264a+304=0\Rightarrow7a^2-33a+38=0\)
Step 4: \((7a-19)(a-2)=0\Rightarrow a=2\ \ (a\in\mathbb Z)\)
Worked derivation: \[a=2,\qquad\bar x=\frac{13}5\]
Check: \[\frac{2+18+25}5-\left(\frac{13}5\right)^2=9-\frac{169}{25}=\frac{56}{25}\]
Why: \(\text{a frequency is a non-negative integer}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=\tfrac{19}7\notin\mathbb Z\); (C) \(3=\tfrac{1+3+5}3\ (\text{unweighted})\); (D) \(a=1:\ \sigma^2=\tfrac{32}{16}=2\ne\tfrac{56}{25}\).
Key point: \(\sigma^2=\overline{x^2}-\bar x^2\ \text{with frequency weights}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A principal cosine inverse produces two distinct signed branches before inverse-angle values are summed
questions.syllabus_anchor: Inverse Trigonometric Functions: principal values; branch analysis
questions.question: Using principal arcsin in [-π/2,π/2] and arccos in [0,π], consider all distinct real solutions of \(\arcsin x+\arccos(2x^2-1)=2\pi/3\). What is the sum of arcsin x over those solutions?
options: A) π/3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2π/9.
Given: \(\arcsin x+\arccos(2x^2-1)=\tfrac{2\pi}3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\theta=\arcsin x\in\left[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right]:\ 2x^2-1=-\cos2\theta;\quad\arccos(-c)=\pi-\arccos c;\quad\arccos(\cos2\theta)=2|\theta|\)
Step 1: \(\arccos(2x^2-1)=\pi-2|\theta|\)
Step 2: \(\theta+\pi-2|\theta|=\tfrac{2\pi}3\)
Step 3: \(\theta\ge0:\ \pi-\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}3\Rightarrow\theta=\tfrac\pi3\)
Step 4: \(\theta<0:\ \pi+3\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}3\Rightarrow\theta=-\tfrac\pi9\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum\arcsin x=\frac\pi3-\frac\pi9=\frac{2\pi}9\]
Check: \[\theta=\tfrac\pi3:\ x=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2,\ \arccos\tfrac12=\tfrac\pi3,\ \tfrac\pi3+\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac{2\pi}3;\quad\theta=-\tfrac\pi9:\ -\tfrac\pi9+\left(\pi-\tfrac{2\pi}9\right)=\tfrac{2\pi}3\]
Why: \(|\theta|\ \text{gives one linear equation for each sign of}\ \theta\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac\pi3\ (\theta\ge0\ \text{only})\); (B) \(-\tfrac\pi9\ (\theta<0\ \text{only})\); (C) \(\tfrac\pi3+\tfrac\pi9=\tfrac{4\pi}9\ (\text{sign lost})\).
Key point: \(\arccos(\cos\phi)=|\phi|\ \text{for}\ |\phi|\le\pi\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Subtractive cancellation controls precision in a later density quotient
questions.syllabus_anchor: Units and Measurements: significant figures; arithmetic with measurements
questions.question: Two measured masses are 20.600 g and 20.584 g. Their difference is divided by a measured volume 0.0250 cm3. Using the usual decimal-place rule for subtraction and significant-figure rule for division, what density should be reported without rounding the masses prematurely?
options: A) 0.6400 g cm−3, four significant figures
B) 0.6 g cm−3, one significant figure
C) 0.64 g cm−3, two significant figures
D) 0 g cm−3, because the rounded masses are equal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.64 g cm−3, two significant figures.
Given: \(m_1=20.600\ \mathrm g,\quad m_2=20.584\ \mathrm g,\quad V=0.0250\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\rho=\dfrac{m_1-m_2}V;\quad\text{subtraction: least decimal places; division: least significant figures}\)
Step 1: \(\Delta m=20.600-20.584=0.016\ \mathrm g\ \ (3\ \text{d.p.}\Rightarrow2\ \text{s.f.})\)
Step 2: \(V=0.0250\ \mathrm{cm^3}\ \ (3\ \text{s.f.})\)
Step 3: \(\rho=\dfrac{0.016}{0.0250}=0.640\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\rho=0.64\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\ \ (2\ \text{s.f.})\]
Check: \[0.64\times0.0250=0.016\ \mathrm g\]
Why: \(\text{subtracting nearly equal numbers reduces the significant figures from 5 to 2}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4\ \text{s.f.}>2\ \text{s.f.}\); (B) \(1\ \text{s.f.}<2\ \text{s.f.}\); (D) \(20.6-20.6=0\ (\text{rounded too early})\).
Key point: \(\text{round only the final result}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Opposite static-friction directions produce lower and upper banked-road speed limits
questions.syllabus_anchor: Laws of Motion: circular motion; friction; banked roads
questions.question: A road of radius 20 m is banked at 45 degrees. The coefficient of static friction is 1/3 and g=10 m s−2. What is the complete speed range for a vehicle to maintain the same horizontal circular path without slipping? Treat the car as a particle and allow static friction to act in either direction.
options: D) v=10√2 m s−1 only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The permitted interval is 10 to 20 m s⁻¹.
Given: Radius r=20 m, bank angle θ=45 degrees and μ=1/3.
Formula/Principle: At each limiting speed static friction is μN, with opposite directions at the two limits.
Step 1: At maximum speed friction acts down the bank: \[N\sin\theta+\mu N\cos\theta=mv_{max}^2/r,\quad N\cos\theta-\mu N\sin\theta=mg.\]
Step 2: Their ratio gives \[v_{max}^2=rg\frac{\tan\theta+\mu}{1-\mu\tan\theta}=200(2)=400.\]
Step 3: At minimum speed friction acts up the bank, giving \[v_{min}^2=rg\frac{\tan\theta-\mu}{1+\mu\tan\theta}=200(1/2)=100.\]
Worked derivation: \[v_{min}=10,\quad v_{max}=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\]
Why: At low speed friction prevents inward/down-bank slip; at high speed it helps provide extra inward force. One friction direction cannot describe both limits.
Why not the others: (A) omits the low-speed slip limit. (C) incorrectly treats the frictionless design speed as the upper limit. (D) excludes the range made possible by static friction.
Key point: Derive both limiting force balances before reporting a banked-road range.
questions.image_alt: The road rises outward, with normal force tilted inward and weight vertical.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Longitudinal extension and transverse contraction jointly change an elastic wire's resistance
questions.syllabus_anchor: Mechanical Properties of Solids: elastic modulus; Current Electricity: resistance
questions.question: A uniform wire has original area 1.00 mm2, Young modulus 2.0×10^11 Pa and resistance 10.0 ohm. It is stretched elastically to longitudinal strain 0.010. In a first-order small-strain model its volume and resistivity are constant. What tensile force and resistance, to first order in strain, follow?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2000 N; 10.2 ohm.
Given: \(A=1.00\ \mathrm{mm^2}=1.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2},\quad Y=2.0\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa},\quad R=10.0\ \Omega,\quad\varepsilon=0.010\)
Formula/Principle: \(F=YA\varepsilon;\quad R=\dfrac{\rho L}A,\quad AL=\text{constant}\)
Step 1: \(F=(2.0\times10^{11})(1.00\times10^{-6})(0.010)=2000\ \mathrm N\)
Step 2: \(L'=L(1+\varepsilon),\quad A'=\dfrac A{1+\varepsilon}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{R'}R=\dfrac{L'}L\cdot\dfrac A{A'}=(1+\varepsilon)^2\approx1+2\varepsilon=1.020\)
Worked derivation: \[F=2000\ \mathrm N,\qquad R'=10.0\times1.020=10.2\ \Omega\]
Check: \[(1.010)^2=1.0201\Rightarrow R'=10.201\ \Omega\approx10.2\ \Omega;\quad\frac FA=2.0\times10^9\ \mathrm{Pa}=Y\varepsilon\]
Why: \(\text{the wire gets longer and thinner; both raise}\ R\)
Why not the others: (B) \(10.1\ \Omega=R(1+\varepsilon)\ (\text{area change ignored})\); (C) \(200\ \mathrm N=\tfrac{2000}{10}\); (D) \(9.8\ \Omega=R(1-2\varepsilon)\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{\Delta R}R=2\dfrac{\Delta L}L\ \text{at constant volume and resistivity}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Removal of one parallel heat-loss channel shifts the steady radiative temperature
questions.syllabus_anchor: Thermal Properties of Matter: heat transfer; radiation; thermal balance
questions.question: A body at steady temperature T0 receives 10 W and loses 6 W by conduction, with the remaining loss by thermal radiation to a fixed environment. The conductive link is removed, incident power remains 10 W and radiation increases monotonically with body temperature. Which statement follows?
options: A) Radiation was 6 W, and the new steady temperature is lower
B) Radiation was 4 W, and the temperature must remain T0
C) Radiation was 10 W, and no temperature adjustment is needed
D) Radiation was 4 W, and the new steady temperature is higher than T0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Radiation was 4 W, and the new steady temperature is higher than T0.
Given: \(P_{\text{in}}=10\ \mathrm W,\quad P_{\text{cond}}=6\ \mathrm W,\quad P_{\text{rad}}(T)\ \text{increasing in}\ T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{steady state}:\ P_{\text{in}}=P_{\text{cond}}+P_{\text{rad}}\)
Step 1: \(P_{\text{rad}}(T_0)=10-6=4\ \mathrm W\)
Step 2: \(\text{link removed, at}\ T_0:\ \dfrac{dU}{dt}=10-4=+6\ \mathrm W>0\Rightarrow T\ \text{rises}\)
Step 3: \(\text{new steady state}:\ P_{\text{rad}}(T_{\text{new}})=10\ \mathrm W\)
Worked derivation: \[P_{\text{rad}}(T_{\text{new}})=10\ \mathrm W>4\ \mathrm W=P_{\text{rad}}(T_0)\Rightarrow T_{\text{new}}>T_0\]
Check: \[\text{before}:\ 10=6+4;\qquad\text{after}:\ 10=0+10\]
Why: \(\text{the remaining loss channel must carry the whole input}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(6\ \mathrm W\ \text{was the conduction loss}\); (B) \(\text{at}\ T_0:\ 10\ne4\); (C) \(10\ \mathrm W\ \text{ignores the}\ 6\ \mathrm W\ \text{conducted}\).
Key point: \(\text{steady state means power in}=\text{power out}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Equal thermodynamic states need not have equal laboratory molecular energy when one gas drifts
questions.syllabus_anchor: Kinetic Theory: ideal-gas pressure; molecular energy; relative motion
questions.question: Two dilute packets of the same monatomic ideal gas have the same rest-frame pressure and number density. Packet A has zero mean laboratory velocity. Packet B has uniform laboratory drift speed U equal to its thermal rms speed w relative to its own mean motion. What is the ratio of mean molecular kinetic energy in the laboratory, B divided by A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2.
Given: \(p_A=p_B,\ n_A=n_B;\quad\vec V_A=0,\quad|\vec V_B|=U=w\ \ (w=\text{thermal rms speed})\)
Formula/Principle: \(p=nkT;\quad\vec v=\vec U+\vec c,\ \langle\vec c\rangle=0\Rightarrow\langle v^2\rangle=U^2+\langle c^2\rangle\)
Step 1: \(T_A=\dfrac p{nk}=T_B\Rightarrow\langle c^2\rangle_A=\langle c^2\rangle_B=w^2\)
Step 2: \(\langle v_A^2\rangle=w^2\)
Step 3: \(\langle v_B^2\rangle=U^2+2\vec U\cdot\langle\vec c\rangle+w^2=w^2+0+w^2=2w^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\langle K_B\rangle}{\langle K_A\rangle}=\frac{\tfrac12m(2w^2)}{\tfrac12mw^2}=2\]
Check: \[\langle K_B\rangle=\tfrac12mU^2+\tfrac32kT=\tfrac32kT+\tfrac32kT\quad\left(\tfrac12mw^2=\tfrac32kT\right)\]
Why: \(\text{pressure and temperature measure only the random part of the motion}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\ (U^2\ \text{omitted})\); (C) \(\sqrt2=\tfrac{v_{rms,B}}{v_{rms,A}}\); (D) \(4=\tfrac{(U+w)^2}{w^2}\).
Key point: \(\langle K\rangle_{\text{lab}}=\tfrac12mU^2+\tfrac32kT\)

questions.sub_topic: A delayed same-frequency contribution changes the resultant SHM amplitude through phase
questions.syllabus_anchor: Oscillations: simple harmonic motion; superposition
questions.question: Two measured displacements are added. The first is x1=A cos(ωt). At time τ=T/3, where T=2π/ω, a second independent oscillator begins contributing x2=A cos[ω(t-τ)]. For t≥τ, what is the amplitude of x1+x2? The addition is a superposition of two signals, not an impulsive change to either oscillator.
options: A) 2A
B) √3 A
C) A
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A.
Given: \(x_1=A\cos\omega t,\quad x_2=A\cos[\omega(t-\tau)],\quad\tau=\dfrac T3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\cos P+\cos Q=2\cos\dfrac{P-Q}2\cos\dfrac{P+Q}2\)
Step 1: \(\phi=\omega\tau=\dfrac{2\pi}T\cdot\dfrac T3=\dfrac{2\pi}3\)
Step 2: \(x_1+x_2=2A\cos\dfrac\phi2\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac\phi2\right)\)
Step 3: \(\cos\dfrac\phi2=\cos\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[A_{\text{res}}=2A\cdot\tfrac12=A\]
Check: \[A_{\text{res}}^2=A^2+A^2+2A^2\cos\tfrac{2\pi}3=2A^2-A^2=A^2\]
Why: \(\text{the two maxima are separated by one third of a period}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2A\ (\phi=0)\); (B) \(\sqrt3A\ (\phi=\tfrac\pi3)\); (D) \(0\ (\phi=\pi)\).
Key point: \(A_{\text{res}}=2A\left|\cos\tfrac\phi2\right|\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Two different end reflections determine pulse sign and successive return times
questions.syllabus_anchor: Waves: reflection; fixed and free boundaries; propagation time
questions.question: A short upward pulse starts at the midpoint of an ideal string, moving right. The left end is fixed and the right end is free; speed is v and total length L. Neglect losses and pulse overlap away from an end. What are the signs of the first two returned pulses observed at the midpoint and their arrival times measured from launch?
options: A) First upward at L/v; second downward at 2L/v
B) First downward at L/v; second upward at 2L/v
C) Both downward, at L/(2v) and L/v
D) Both upward, at L/v and 2L/v
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) First upward at L/v; second downward at 2L/v.
Given: \(\text{pulse}\ (+)\ \text{from}\ x=\tfrac L2\ \text{moving right};\quad\text{left end fixed, right end free}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{free end}:\ +\to+;\quad\text{fixed end}:\ +\to-;\quad t=\dfrac dv\)
Step 1: \(d_1=\tfrac L2+\tfrac L2=L\Rightarrow t_1=\dfrac Lv,\quad\text{sign}=+\)
Step 2: \(d_2=L+\tfrac L2+\tfrac L2=2L\Rightarrow t_2=\dfrac{2L}v,\quad\text{sign}=-\)
Worked derivation: \[(t_1,\text{sign}_1)=\left(\tfrac Lv,+\right),\qquad(t_2,\text{sign}_2)=\left(\tfrac{2L}v,-\right)\]
Check: \[t_2-t_1=\frac Lv=\frac{2(L/2)}v\ \ (\text{midpoint}\to\text{fixed end}\to\text{midpoint})\]
Why: \(y=0\ \text{at a fixed end forces inversion};\quad\tfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}=0\ \text{at a free end does not}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{free and fixed rules interchanged}\); (C) \(\tfrac L{2v}\ \text{is a one-way time}\); (D) \(\text{fixed-end inversion omitted}\).
Key point: \(\text{fixed end inverts, free end does not}\)

questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.sub_topic: A fixed Gaussian surface changes flux when charges exchange inside and outside positions
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electric Charges and Fields: electric flux; Gauss's law
questions.question: At stage X a closed Gaussian surface encloses +q while a separate -2q charge lies outside. At stage Y the +q charge is outside and -2q is inside; neither charge lies on the surface in either stage. The surface geometry is unchanged. What is final outward electric flux minus initial outward electric flux?
options: B) -q/ε0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The flux change is -3q/ε0.
Given: Charge positions relative to the surface change while its area does not.
Formula/Principle: Net outward electric flux is enclosed charge divided by ε0.
Step 1: \[\Phi_X=q/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\Phi_Y=-2q/\varepsilon_0.\]
Step 2: \[\Delta\Phi=\Phi_Y-\Phi_X=-3q/\varepsilon_0.\]
Worked derivation: The same signed result follows from +q leaving and -2q entering: \(\Delta Q_{inside}=-q-2q=-3q\).
Why: External charges can change the field on parts of a surface without adding net enclosed charge. Surface area alone does not fix the flux.
Why not the others: (A) reverses final minus initial. (B) combines the two charge values without tracking which side contains them. (C) assumes unchanged geometry implies unchanged flux.
Key point: Track signed charge crossing the boundary, not only surface area.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Kirchhoff's junction rule and conservation of charge
questions.syllabus_anchor: Current Electricity: potentiometer; internal resistance
questions.question: Four wires meet at a junction in a steady-current circuit. Currents of 2.0 A and 3.0 A flow into the junction through two of the wires, and 4.0 A flows out through the third. What is the current in the fourth wire, and which conservation law does the rule used express?
options: A) 1.0 A into the junction; conservation of energy
B) 1.0 A out of the junction; conservation of charge
C) 9.0 A out of the junction; conservation of charge
D) 1.0 A out of the junction; conservation of energy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.0 A out of the junction; conservation of charge.
Given: \(I_{\text{in}}=2.0\ \mathrm A,\ 3.0\ \mathrm A;\quad I_{\text{out}}=4.0\ \mathrm A;\quad\text{steady currents}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\sum I_{\text{in}}=\sum I_{\text{out}}\)
Step 1: \(2.0+3.0=4.0+I_4\)
Worked derivation: \[I_4=5.0-4.0=1.0\ \mathrm A\ \ (\text{out of the junction})\]
Check: \[\text{in}:\ 5.0\ \mathrm A;\quad\text{out}:\ 4.0+1.0=5.0\ \mathrm A\]
Why: \(\text{no charge accumulates at a junction in a steady state}\Rightarrow\dfrac{dq}{dt}=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(I_4\ \text{into the junction}:\ 6.0\ \mathrm A\ne4.0\ \mathrm A\); (C) \(9.0=2.0+3.0+4.0\) (all currents added); (D) \(\text{energy conservation gives the loop rule},\ \sum\Delta V=0\).
Key point: \(\text{junction rule}:\ \text{charge};\quad\text{loop rule}:\ \text{energy}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: An inductor can return energy with unchanged current direction and reversed terminal voltage
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electromagnetic Induction: self-inductance; energy
questions.question: The ideal inductor in the diagram has current I=I0 sin(ωt) entering terminal A and leaving B. At t=3π/(4ω), which signs describe I, terminal voltage VA-VB and the rate of change of its stored energy?
options: A) I positive; voltage positive; energy increasing
B) I negative; voltage negative; energy increasing
C) I positive; voltage negative; energy decreasing
D) I positive; voltage zero; energy constant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Current remains positive, voltage is negative and stored energy is falling.
Given: The terminal voltage uses the passive convention, with current entering A.
Formula/Principle: \(V_A-V_B=L\,dI/dt\) and \(dU/dt=LI\,dI/dt\).
Step 1: At ωt=3π/4, \[I=I_0/\sqrt2>0,\quad dI/dt=-\omega I_0/\sqrt2<0.\]
Step 2: \[V_A-V_B=-L\omega I_0/\sqrt2<0.\]
Worked derivation: \[dU/dt=-L\omega I_0^2/2<0.\]
Why: Voltage sign responds to the change of current, not to current sign alone. Here the inductor returns magnetic energy while current still flows in its original direction.
Why not the others: (A) assigns the increasing-current signs. (B) confuses negative slope with negative current. (D) uses the current maximum time instead of the stated time.
Key point: Distinguish current, current derivative and energy-flow signs.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Loaded transformer terminal voltage and efficiency include winding and core losses
questions.syllabus_anchor: Alternating Current: transformers; power and efficiency
questions.question: A transformer model uses the ideal induced-emf turns relation with Np/Ns=5 and primary voltage 100 V rms. Its secondary winding has resistance 1 ohm and supplies a 4 ohm resistor. Core loss is 20 W and all other losses are neglected. What are the delivered load power and efficiency?
options: A) 80 W; 80 percent
B) 64 W; 80 percent
C) 100 W; 64 percent
D) 64 W; 64 percent
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 64 W; 64 percent.
Given: \(\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}=5,\quad V_p=100\ \mathrm V,\quad r_s=1\ \Omega,\quad R_L=4\ \Omega,\quad P_{\text{core}}=20\ \mathrm W\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_s=V_p\dfrac{N_s}{N_p},\quad I_s=\dfrac{E_s}{r_s+R_L},\quad\eta=\dfrac{P_{\text{load}}}{P_{\text{load}}+P_{\text{Cu}}+P_{\text{core}}}\)
Step 1: \(E_s=\dfrac{100}5=20\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(I_s=\dfrac{20}{1+4}=4\ \mathrm A\)
Step 3: \(P_{\text{load}}=4^2\times4=64\ \mathrm W\)
Step 4: \(P_{\text{Cu}}=4^2\times1=16\ \mathrm W\)
Worked derivation: \[\eta=\frac{64}{64+16+20}=\frac{64}{100}=64\%\]
Check: \[E_sI_s=20\times4=80\ \mathrm W=64+16;\quad P_{\text{in}}=80+20=100\ \mathrm W\]
Why: \(\text{the load voltage is}\ 20-4\times1=16\ \mathrm V,\ \text{not}\ 20\ \mathrm V\)
Why not the others: (A) \(80\ \mathrm W=E_sI_s\); (B) \(\tfrac{64}{80}=80\%\ (\text{core loss omitted})\); (C) \(100\ \mathrm W=P_{\text{in}}\).
Key point: \(\eta=\dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{output}+\text{all losses}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Eyepiece translation changes telescope image distance and angular magnification
questions.syllabus_anchor: Ray Optics: telescope; lens formula; angular magnification
questions.question: An astronomical telescope has objective focal length 80 cm and eyepiece focal length 5 cm. It is initially normally adjusted for a distant object. The eyepiece alone is moved 1 cm toward the objective. What are the final image distance measured from the eyepiece with Cartesian signs and the magnitude of the angular magnification? Use paraxial angles and an eye close to the eyepiece.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) -20 cm; 20.
Given: \(f_o=80\ \mathrm{cm},\quad f_e=5\ \mathrm{cm},\quad\text{eyepiece moved}\ 1\ \mathrm{cm}\ \text{toward the objective}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f;\quad M=\dfrac\beta\alpha\)
Step 1: \(\text{normal adjustment}:\ d=80+5=85\ \mathrm{cm};\quad d'=84\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(u_e=-(84-80)=-4\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac15+\dfrac1{-4}=-\dfrac1{20}\Rightarrow v=-20\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 4: \(\alpha=\dfrac h{f_o}=\dfrac h{80},\quad\beta=\dfrac h{|u_e|}=\dfrac h4\)
Worked derivation: \[v=-20\ \mathrm{cm},\qquad|M|=\frac{h/4}{h/80}=20\]
Check: \[h'=\frac vuh=5h,\quad\beta=\frac{5h}{20}=\frac h4;\quad|M|=\frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1+\frac{f_e}{|v|}\right)=16\times\frac54=20\]
Why: \(\text{the objective image stays at 80 cm; only the eyepiece setting changes}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(v<0\ (\text{virtual})\); (C) \(16=\tfrac{f_o}{f_e}\ (\text{normal adjustment})\); (D) \(-4\ \mathrm{cm}=u_e\).
Key point: \(|M|=\dfrac{f_o}{|u_e|}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Coincident diffraction zeros remove interference orders at the central-envelope boundary
questions.syllabus_anchor: Wave Optics: interference; single-slit diffraction
questions.question: Two identical slits of width a have centre separation d=3a. Use interference maxima d sinθ=mλ and single-slit diffraction minima a sinθ=nλ, with nonzero integer n. Which is the first missing noncentral interference order, and how many bright interference maxima remain strictly inside the central diffraction envelope?
options: A) Second order; three maxima
B) Third order; seven maxima
C) Third order; five maxima
D) Sixth order; five maxima
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The third order is first missing and five interference maxima lie inside the central envelope.
Given: The diffraction envelope's first minima occur at |a sinθ|=λ.
Formula/Principle: A nominal interference maximum disappears when it coincides with a diffraction minimum.
Step 1: Equating the two angular conditions gives \[m\lambda/d=n\lambda/a\ \Rightarrow\ m=3n.\] The first nonzero missing order is |m|=3.
Step 2: Strictly within the central envelope, \(|m|<d/a=3\).
Worked derivation: Allowed bright orders are \[-2,-1,0,1,2,\] giving five.
Why: The envelope boundary orders ±3 cannot be counted as bright because the individual-slit amplitude vanishes there.
Why not the others: (A) confuses d/a with another order relation. (B) counts the extinguished boundary maxima. (D) skips the first coincident diffraction zero.
Key point: Apply the interference condition together with the finite-slit envelope.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: A fixed total energy makes wavelength-product minimisation different from equal-momentum allocation
questions.syllabus_anchor: Dual Nature: matter wavelengths; kinetic energy; constrained quadratic maximum
questions.question: Two nonrelativistic particles have masses m and 4m and freely adjustable positive kinetic energies KA,KB with fixed sum K. Which division minimises the product of their de Broglie wavelengths, and what is λA/λB at that minimum?
options: A) KA=4K/5, KB=K/5; ratio 1
B) KA=KB=K/2; ratio 2
C) KA=KB=K/2; ratio 1
D) KA=K/5, KB=4K/5; ratio 4
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) KA=KB=K/2; ratio 2.
Given: \(m_A=m,\quad m_B=4m,\quad K_A+K_B=K\)
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda=\dfrac h{\sqrt{2mK}}\)
Step 1: \(\lambda_A\lambda_B=\dfrac{h^2}{\sqrt{2mK_A}\sqrt{8mK_B}}=\dfrac{h^2}{4m\sqrt{K_AK_B}}\)
Step 2: \(K_AK_B=K_A(K-K_A)=\dfrac{K^2}4-\left(K_A-\dfrac K2\right)^2\le\dfrac{K^2}4\)
Step 3: \(\text{maximum at}\ K_A=K_B=\dfrac K2\)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B}=\sqrt{\dfrac{m_BK_B}{m_AK_A}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{4m}m}=2\)
Worked derivation: \[K_A=K_B=\frac K2,\qquad\frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B}=2,\qquad(\lambda_A\lambda_B)_{\min}=\frac{h^2}{2mK}\]
Check: \[K_A=\tfrac{4K}5,\ K_B=\tfrac K5:\ \sqrt{K_AK_B}=\tfrac{2K}5<\tfrac K2\Rightarrow\lambda_A\lambda_B=\tfrac{5h^2}{8mK}>\tfrac{h^2}{2mK}\]
Why: \(\text{a fixed sum gives the largest product at equal shares}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{equal momenta, but}\ \tfrac58>\tfrac12\); (C) \(\text{equal}\ K,\ \text{unequal}\ m\Rightarrow\lambda_A\ne\lambda_B\); (D) \(\sqrt{K_AK_B}=\tfrac{2K}5<\tfrac K2\).
Key point: \(\lambda\propto\dfrac1{\sqrt{mK}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Donor ionisation changes majority carriers while fixed-ion compensation preserves bulk neutrality
questions.syllabus_anchor: Semiconductor Electronics: extrinsic semiconductor; donors; charge neutrality
questions.question: A silicon crystal is doped with dilute pentavalent donors. In a uniform bulk region each donor is ionised once, no external charge has been added, and electron concentration greatly exceeds hole concentration. Which description preserves both carrier identity and bulk charge accounting?
options: A) The bulk must be negatively charged because mobile electrons are majority carriers
B) Positive donor ions move through the crystal as its main current carriers
C) The ionised donors are negatively charged and holes are the majority carriers
D) Electrons are majority mobile carriers; positive fixed donor ions balance their excess charge approximately in the neutral bulk
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Electrons are majority mobile carriers; positive fixed donor ions balance their excess charge approximately in the neutral bulk.
Given: \(\text{Si with donors}\ N_D\ (\text{all ionised}),\quad n\gg p,\quad\text{no net charge added}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathrm D\to\mathrm D^++e^-;\quad\rho=e\left(p+N_D^+-n\right)\)
Step 1: \(\text{each donor}:\ \text{one mobile}\ e^-\ \text{and one fixed}\ \mathrm D^+\)
Step 2: \(\rho=0\Rightarrow n=p+N_D^+\)
Step 3: \(n\gg p\Rightarrow n\approx N_D^+\)
Worked derivation: \[\rho=e\left(p+N_D^+-n\right)\approx0,\qquad n\approx N_D\gg p\]
Check: \[np=n_i^2\Rightarrow p=\frac{n_i^2}{N_D}\ll n_i\ll n\]
Why: \(\text{n-type names the majority carrier, not the net charge}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\rho\approx0,\ \text{not}\ <0\); (B) \(\mathrm D^+\ \text{ions are bound to the lattice}\); (C) \(\text{donor ions are}\ +,\ \text{and}\ n\gg p\).
Key point: \(\text{doping changes carrier numbers, not the net charge}\)
